scale: -2 = strongly disagree, -1 = disagree, 0 = neutral/mixed, +1 = agree, +2 = strongly agree; null = the party has no public position we could find (never guessed). Positions are the party's, relative to the statement text.
blind: Statement text and explainers are written without party names or branded policy names (enforced by quiz_build.py), so voters answer on the substance. Party positions and evidence are shown only after answering.

scoring.method: For each statement both the user and the party answered: agreement = 1 - |user - party| / 4. Weighted average over those statements using user importance weights (default 1; suggest 0.5/1/2). Report coverage = statements the party has a position on, out of statements the user answered; flag matches with coverage below 10 statements, and blend toward 0.5 (neutral) by adjusted = (sum_w*agree + k*0.5) / (sum_w + k) with k = 3 so thin records are not over-rewarded.

statements.text: Profits from selling investment property and commercial property should be taxed, with the family home exempt.
statements.explainer: New Zealand has no general tax on capital gains. A tax like this would apply when an investor or business sells property for more than they paid, raising money for public services; opponents say it discourages investment and is complex to run.

national.evidence: "No new taxes, including no capital gains tax."

labour.evidence: Create a 28% capital gains tax on commercial and residential property, excluding the family home, from 1 July 2027.

green.evidence: Prefers wider wealth taxes; Green MP Teanau Tuiono called Labour's CGT "quite narrow" and said the Greens' wealth tax would be more effective. Greens also propose a 33% capital acquisitions (inheritance/gift) tax and reversing the brightline-test changes (KPMG tracker).

act.evidence: KPMG 2026 tax tracker lists ACT: "No capital gains tax" (plus a crypto capital-gains exemption).

alliance.evidence: "The Alliance will introduce a broad-based capital gains tax, covering investment property, shares..." (33%, excluding the family home).

statements.text: People with very large fortunes (for example net wealth above several million dollars) should pay an annual wealth tax.
statements.explainer: A wealth tax charges a small percentage each year on the total value of what someone owns (property, shares, businesses) above a high threshold. Supporters say it funds services and reduces inequality; opponents say it is hard to value assets and may push wealthy people and capital offshore.

national.evidence: National's Economic Plan lists the Greens/Te Pāti Māori "Asset Tax" among "nine new taxes" it opposes; promises "no new taxes".

labour.evidence: KPMG tracker: "Chris Hipkins has ruled out a wealth/inheritance tax."

green.evidence: Introduce a 2.5% tax on net wealth over $10 million (family homes exempt).

act.evidence: KPMG tracker lists ACT: "No wealth tax/inheritance tax."

nz-first.evidence: KPMG tracker: NZ First position "Not stated, has previously opposed such taxes."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Implement a targeted wealth tax: 1.5% on net assets $2–5m, 2% on $5–10m, 2.5% over $10m ("A Kiwi Tax Plan").

alliance.evidence: "2.5% Wealth Tax: An annual tax on individual net wealth above $2 million."

statements.text: GST should be taken off food such as fresh fruit and vegetables.
statements.explainer: GST is charged at 15% on almost all food. Removing it would lower prices at the checkout if retailers pass the saving on, but would cost the government around a billion dollars a year and make the tax system more complicated.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Remove GST costs from kai" — delivered as an income-tax "Kai Credit" worth about eight weeks of groceries for people earning under $60,000, rather than a GST exemption at the till.

animal-justice.evidence: "Remove GST from fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts and other core plant-based foods."

conservative.evidence: Favours a lower overall GST rate (12.5%) rather than food exemptions: "A lower rate of GST -12.5% is favoured."

statements.text: The first slice of everyone's income (for example the first $10,000 or more) should be tax-free.
statements.explainer: Income is currently taxed from the first dollar. A tax-free threshold gives every earner the same dollar saving, which is worth more to low earners in percentage terms; it has to be paid for by other taxes or by cutting spending.

green.evidence: Make the first $10,000 people earn tax-free.

nz-first.evidence: KPMG tracker: NZ First would "make the lowest tax bracket (currently $14,000 pa) of income tax-free no later than 1 April 2027."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Make the first $30,000 earned tax-free.

alliance.evidence: "Make the first $20,000 of every person's income completely tax-free."

vision-nz.evidence: "Make the first $25,000 of personal income completely tax-free."

statements.text: The government should force the two big supermarket groups to be broken up or restructured so more chains compete.
statements.explainer: Two groups own almost all supermarkets. Options range from making them sell off stores to a new competitor, through to a state-owned chain, versus simply making it easier for new entrants to set up. Breaking them up may lower prices but is legally and practically hard.

national.evidence: Separate the Foodstuffs business into two nationwide cooperatives (a targeted restructure rather than a full break-up).

labour.evidence: Separate wholesale food businesses from the retail supermarket sector.

green.evidence: Break up the supermarket duopoly and use part of it to create a government-owned supermarket.

act.evidence: "While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives, ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter."

nz-first.evidence: Separate the Foodstuffs supermarket chain into two national cooperatives and give the Grocery Commissioner more powers.

opportunity.evidence: Give the Commerce Commission greater powers and more market support to small businesses (no specific break-up).

statements.text: The minimum wage should rise every year by at least the rate of inflation.
statements.explainer: Automatic increases protect the lowest-paid from rising prices. Smaller or frozen increases make it cheaper to employ people and, some argue, protect jobs for young and low-skilled workers.

labour.evidence: Increase the minimum wage every year; answered "Yes" to NZCTU: set the minimum wage above inflation for the next 3 years.

green.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

act.evidence: Freeze the minimum wage for three years.

nz-first.evidence: Increase the minimum wage in line with inflation; answered "Yes" to the NZCTU scorecard question.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

alliance.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

womens-rights.evidence: "Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes."

vision-nz.evidence: "Legislate the transition from the minimum wage to an annually adjusted Living Wage to protect working families from inflation."

statements.text: Pay and conditions should be able to be set for a whole industry at once (for example all cleaners or all supermarket workers) through compulsory bargaining between unions and employers.
statements.explainer: Today pay is mostly set workplace by workplace or individually. Industry-wide agreements would set a floor for everyone in that job, lifting pay in low-wage sectors; employers say they remove flexibility and push up costs.

national.evidence: Repealed the Fair Pay Agreements Act in December 2023 (all National MPs voted for repeal); NZCTU scorecard "No".

labour.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

green.evidence: Reverse changes to pay equity and fair pay agreements; NZCTU scorecard "Yes".

act.evidence: Supported the 2023 repeal; NZCTU scorecard "No".

nz-first.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "No" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

opportunity.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "No" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

alliance.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

womens-rights.evidence: Advocates "reinstatement of legislative support for Fair Pay Agreements."

statements.text: There should be a legal limit on how much a landlord can raise the rent each year.
statements.explainer: Rent can currently rise by any amount, but only once every 12 months. A cap (for example tied to inflation) protects existing tenants from large jumps; critics say it discourages new rentals and maintenance.

national.evidence: Focuses on building more homes "rather than controlling rents" (Salient 2026 guide); points to rent increases at a 25-year low.

labour.evidence: In 2023 Chris Hipkins ruled out the Greens' rent cap, saying it was not under consideration "and would not be in the future"; Labour's 2026 rent pledge covers only state/social housing tenants.

green.evidence: Limit annual rent increases to 2 percent.

act.evidence: Favours increasing supply through deregulation and property rights "rather than measures such as rent controls" (Salient 2026 guide).

alliance.evidence: Caps social-housing rent at 25% of income (state-owned housing only).

statements.text: The government should build a lot more state and public housing itself.
statements.explainer: State houses are owned by the government and rented at income-related rents. Building many more costs billions up front but houses people on the waiting list directly; the alternative is relying on community housing providers and private developers.

national.evidence: "Focused primarily on building more homes rather than controlling rents... free up land, streamline planning and consenting" — supply-led, not a state building programme (Salient guide).

labour.evidence: Add at least 6,000 more social housing places over the next four years.

green.evidence: Increase public housing supply and housing support.

act.evidence: Favours "increasing supply through deregulation, stronger property rights and easier consenting" and "greater faith in private investment... than in direct government provision".

te-pati-maori.evidence: Increase the supply of housing in both the public and private sector; wants more public and affordable housing.

alliance.evidence: "A five-year housing plan: a massive public building programme led by Kāinga Ora, alongside a newly established Ministry of Works."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Mana Taumaru local build policy: hemp-panel homes built by local trainees on papakāinga, allocated to families in overcrowded or substandard housing.

statements.text: Councils should have to allow more and denser housing, such as townhouses and apartments, in our cities.
statements.explainer: Zoning rules decide how many homes can be built and how tall. Requiring more density tends to lower prices over time and reduce sprawl; some residents object to the change in their neighbourhoods and the strain on pipes and roads.

national.evidence: Wants to "free up land, streamline planning and consenting, and finance the infrastructure needed for development" (Salient guide); removing the ban on minimum car-parking is the only partial exception.

green.evidence: Encourage mixed-use areas and walkability in new housing developments.

act.evidence: Favours increasing supply through deregulation and easier consenting (Salient guide).

opportunity.evidence: Revamp zoning to reduce house prices.

statements.text: Everyone should get some free GP visits each year, paid for by the government.
statements.explainer: Most adults currently pay $20 to $80 or more per GP visit. Free visits would remove a cost barrier to seeing a doctor but would need hundreds of millions of dollars a year and more GPs to meet demand.

national.evidence: Says Labour's "free" promises (including the Medicard) total $18 billion and would need "nine new taxes"; offers rural doctor funding and pharmacist access instead.

labour.evidence: Make up to three GP visits a year free with a Medicard.

green.evidence: Increase free public health services.

alliance.evidence: "Elimination of costs for GP visits, dental, optical, and audiology services."

statements.text: The $5 charge for each prescription should be scrapped for everyone.
statements.explainer: Most adults pay $5 per prescription item, with exemptions for children, Community Services Card holders and over-65s. Removing it for everyone costs roughly $150 million a year; supporters say it stops people skipping medicines, opponents say the money is better targeted.

national.evidence: Keeps the $5 charge it reinstated in 2024 for most adults, with "targeted free prescriptions to seniors" instead of universal free prescriptions.

labour.evidence: Remove the $5 charge for prescriptions (restore universal free prescriptions).

statements.text: Free school lunches should be expanded and made more generous, even if it costs more.
statements.explainer: Schools in poorer areas get a free lunch programme funded at roughly $3 a meal. Expanding it to more schools or spending more per meal costs more each year; supporters point to attendance and learning, opponents to cost and food waste.

labour.evidence: Pay for school lunches that cost $5 per meal and ensure schools provide locally made lunches.

green.evidence: Keep and expand the free school lunches programme.

opportunity.evidence: Rebuild the school lunch programme.

statements.text: Privately run but publicly funded schools (charter schools) should continue to be allowed alongside state schools.
statements.explainer: Charter schools receive government funding per student but are run by private operators with more freedom over curriculum, hours and teacher pay, and less direct oversight. Supporters say they give choice to families poorly served by state schools; opponents say they divert money and lack accountability.

labour.evidence: Labour vowed in 2024 to "get rid of" charter schools if returned to government.

green.evidence: Green alternative Budget 2025 includes "Abolition of Charter Schools Agency".

act.evidence: ACT campaigns on expanding charter schools.

statements.text: University and polytechnic study should be fees-free.
statements.explainer: Students currently borrow fees through the student loan scheme, with limited fees-free support. Making study free costs the government more each year and mostly benefits those who go on to tertiary study; supporters say it widens access and reduces debt.

national.evidence: National's student policy is lowering the student-loan repayment rate to 10%, not fees-free study.

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 student offer is a 10% student-loan cut for graduates who did not get Fees Free, not a return to fees-free study.

green.evidence: Introduce fees-free tertiary education, universal student allowances and paid placements.

alliance.evidence: Platform promises "free education and healthcare" (RNZ summary of the Alliance).

statements.text: Anyone convicted of a third serious violent or sexual offence should get a mandatory longer sentence, with little room for the judge to decide otherwise.
statements.explainer: Mandatory sentencing laws set minimum penalties for repeat offenders. Supporters say they keep dangerous people off the streets and deter crime; critics say they fill prisons, remove judges' discretion and can lead to harsh results in unusual cases.

national.evidence: Voted for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 at every reading.

labour.evidence: Voted against reinstatement; justice spokesperson Duncan Webb said three-strikes regimes did little to reduce serious crime.

green.evidence: Voted against; Tamatha Paul said it would disproportionately target Māori and increase incarceration.

act.evidence: Voted for reinstating three strikes; 2026 policy adds a minimum three-year sentence for a third burglary conviction.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for the Reinstating Three Strikes Amendment Act 2024.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Reinstating Three Strikes Bill.

alliance.evidence: Justice policy reframes it as "Three strikes and into treatment" — prevention and rehabilitation rather than longer sentences.

conservative.evidence: Wants "meaningful consequences for serious and repeat offending" and longer sentences for repeat child sex offenders.

statements.text: We should send fewer people to prison and put more into rehabilitation and community-based sentences.
statements.explainer: New Zealand imprisons more people per head than most comparable countries. Community sentences and rehabilitation cost less per person and may reduce reoffending; opponents say they are too lenient and put victims at risk.

national.evidence: Add 240 beds to Christchurch Men's Prison; backs tougher sentencing (three strikes).

green.evidence: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders; reduce restrictions on judges' decisions.

act.evidence: Tougher sentencing, including a mandatory minimum for a third burglary conviction.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Abolish prisons by 2040 and move towards restorative justice.

opportunity.evidence: Boost court and rehabilitation funding to reduce reoffending.

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "Education not incarceration" — redirect money from prohibition enforcement to health and education.

alliance.evidence: "Three strikes and into treatment. Prevent harm, rehabilitate, support victims."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Prison Sinking Lid Policy" — shift non-violent offenders with addiction and mental-health needs out of prison into localised rehabilitation.

statements.text: Farmers should pay for their greenhouse gas emissions, for example by bringing agriculture into the Emissions Trading Scheme.
statements.explainer: Agriculture produces about half of New Zealand's emissions but, unlike other sectors, does not pay for them. Pricing them encourages lower-emission farming and helps meet climate targets; farmers say it would cut production and send farming offshore.

national.evidence: Maintain the current position of agricultural emissions not being priced or offset through the ETS.

labour.evidence: Made no commitment to price farm emissions: "in government Labour will urgently review the ETS" (Greenpeace survey answer).

green.evidence: "We will bring agricultural emissions into the ETS" (answer to Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme.

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support emissions pricing in any form unless adopted by key trading partners" (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing agriculture into the ETS by mid-2027 (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

opportunity.evidence: Strengthen the ETS and include agriculture; told Greenpeace it "will explore a cap-and-trade market or novel levy structure" for biogenic methane.

animal-justice.evidence: Wants to "redirect funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes" and transition farmers to plant-based agriculture.

alliance.evidence: Replace the ETS with a carbon tax on a polluter-pays principle (no specific farm carve-out stated).

conservative.evidence: "There is no climate emergency... Laws/agreements like the Paris Accord, Zero Carbon Act, and Emissions Trading Scheme impose significant costs."

statements.text: New Zealand should keep its legal target of net-zero emissions by 2050 and stay in the Paris climate agreement.
statements.explainer: The 2050 target is written into law and the Paris agreement commits the country to international emissions pledges. Keeping them means ongoing costs and regulation; leaving or weakening them risks trade and reputational consequences.

labour.evidence: "Labour is fully committed to the Paris Agreement and will put New Zealand on course to meet its targets."

green.evidence: Enforce timely implementation of climate legislation and increase Zero Carbon Act reporting and transparency.

act.evidence: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net-zero goal.

nz-first.evidence: Says it would withdraw New Zealand from the Paris Agreement (Salient guide; KPMG tracker: "Campaigned to leave the Paris Accord").

opportunity.evidence: Retain the Climate Change Commission and ensure NZ's emissions goals align with the Paris Agreement.

nz-loyal.evidence: "End climate accords based on faulty science" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "Let's get out of Paris accord and work for solutions to mitigate weather risks."

conservative.evidence: "New Zealand should leave the Paris Agreement"; all climate legislation "should be repealed or withdrawn".

vision-nz.evidence: "Restore absolute national sovereignty by leaving the United Nations and the Paris Accord."

statements.text: Ministers should be able to approve big infrastructure, mining and development projects through a faster process that bypasses the normal environmental consent system.
statements.explainer: Normally projects need resource consents, with public input and the right to object. A fast-track lets selected projects be decided by expert panels or ministers in months rather than years; supporters say it gets things built, opponents say it cuts out communities and environmental checks.

national.evidence: Passed the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (supported at every reading) and proposes a fast-track policy statement for mining.

labour.evidence: Voted against the Act; "Labour will fix the Fast-track Approvals Act so that environmental protections are not overridden, there is public participation" (keeps a fast-track, but changed).

green.evidence: Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act.

act.evidence: Supported the Fast-track Approvals Act at every reading.

nz-first.evidence: The Act was part of NZ First's coalition agreement; supported at every reading.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Fast-track Approvals Act at all three readings.

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to restoring strong environmental protections and public participation in all resource consenting (Greenpeace survey).

alliance.evidence: Criticises the government for "fast-tracking legislation and using urgency for policies that harm Aotearoa New Zealand".

statements.text: Seabed mining should be banned in New Zealand waters.
statements.explainer: Companies want to mine iron sands and other minerals from the seafloor. A ban protects marine ecosystems and fisheries but forgoes export income and jobs in the regions involved.

national.evidence: Voted against members' bills to ban seabed mining (2023) and created the fast-track pathway used by seabed miners (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

green.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Voted against seabed-mining ban bills (2023); vocal pro-mining stance (Greenpeace assessment).

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support a ban; instead, we advocate for higher government levies on minerals extracted from coastal seabed iron sands."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Ban seabed mining.

opportunity.evidence: Permanently ban seabed mining in NZ waters.

animal-justice.evidence: Key objective: "Restrict seabed mining" (restriction rather than outright ban).

statements.text: New offshore oil and gas exploration should be banned again.
statements.explainer: A ban on new offshore exploration permits was in place for several years and has since been lifted. Reinstating it supports the move away from fossil fuels; opponents say it worsens gas shortages and pushes up power prices.

national.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing back the ban (Greenpeace survey); Hipkins has said Labour would reinstate it while honouring existing permits.

green.evidence: "Yes. The Green Party wants to see new fossil fuel extraction ended in Aotearoa."

act.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

nz-first.evidence: "No. NZ First does not support reinstating a blanket ban on oil and gas exploration."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to reinstating the ban (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Would "not oppose a reinstatement" but considers it "probably unnecessary" and would not progress it itself.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Establish energy independence, including oil and gas" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

animal-justice.evidence: "Reverse the lifting of the offshore exploration ban and reinstate the moratorium on new fossil fuel permits."

conservative.evidence: "Actively encourage commercial oil and gas exploration."

statements.text: The government should take a bigger direct role in electricity, such as setting up a new state-owned power company or splitting the big power companies into separate generators and retailers.
statements.explainer: Four large companies both generate and sell most of New Zealand's electricity. Breaking them up or adding a state competitor aims to lower prices; opponents say it would deter the investment needed for new generation.

national.evidence: The National-led government's 2025 electricity review response did not include structural separation; Nicola Willis argued splitting the gentailers risked "massive instability".

green.evidence: Establish a publicly owned Crown entity ("Kiwipower") to invest in renewable generation.

act.evidence: Open power transmission to private investment; opposes break-ups and state-run alternatives.

nz-first.evidence: Divide the "generation" and "retail" arms of power companies.

opportunity.evidence: Restructure the electricity market to bring prices down; use the Crown's gentailer stakes to fund renewables.

alliance.evidence: "100 percent public ownership of electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail."

statements.text: Parliament should write a single legal definition of the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi, rather than leaving the courts and the Waitangi Tribunal to interpret them case by case.
statements.explainer: The Treaty's "principles" are referred to in many laws but defined by courts and the Tribunal over time. Fixing them in statute would give Parliament the final say and could narrow Māori rights as currently understood; opponents say it rewrites a founding agreement without Māori consent.

national.evidence: Voted against the Bill at its second reading after supporting it only to select committee; Luxon pledged to refuse a Treaty referendum.

labour.evidence: Voted against at both readings; said the Bill's principles "did not match the principles of the Treaty".

green.evidence: Voted against at both readings.

act.evidence: Sponsored the Treaty Principles Bill; its 11 MPs were the only votes in favour at the second reading (10 April 2025).

nz-first.evidence: Voted against at the second reading, but its own policy is to remove references to "the principles of the Treaty" from legislation.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against at both readings; MPs led the haka protest at the first reading.

statements.text: The Waitangi Tribunal should be abolished or replaced once historical claims are settled.
statements.explainer: The Tribunal investigates Crown breaches of the Treaty and makes mostly non-binding recommendations on both historical and current issues. Winding it up would end an independent check on government; supporters say its job is done once settlements finish.

green.evidence: Implement Waitangi Tribunal recommendations; uphold te Tiriti across government decision-making.

act.evidence: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Increase and entrench Waitangi Tribunal funding and extend its binding jurisdiction on the Crown.

statements.text: The Māori electorates should be abolished, or their future put to a referendum.
statements.explainer: Seven seats in Parliament are elected by voters on the Māori roll, guaranteeing Māori representation. Abolishing them, or asking all voters to decide, is argued as treating everyone the same; opponents say only Māori should decide the future of their seats.

green.evidence: Entrench the Māori electoral seats.

nz-first.evidence: Introduce a binding referendum on the Māori seats.

statements.text: Public services such as health should be targeted by need alone, with no programmes aimed specifically at Māori or other ethnic groups.
statements.explainer: Māori have worse outcomes on many measures. One view is that Māori-led or ethnicity-targeted services close those gaps faster; the other is that help should go to whoever needs it most regardless of ethnicity.

labour.evidence: Introduce a Māori-led job training programme and fund; allocate 5% of government procurement to Māori businesses.

green.evidence: Simplify funding for Hauora Māori providers; create a Māori Education Authority.

act.evidence: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services.

nz-first.evidence: Disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board from Auckland Council; policy is to remove "principles of the Treaty" references from environmental laws.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Invest in Māori health outcomes; Māori-led health, education, disability and justice systems.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Scrap all race-based policies" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

alliance.evidence: Māori health providers keep the option to remain independent with full funding; constitutional change with Te Tiriti at the centre.

conservative.evidence: "Employment, promotion and access to public services should be based on individual need, ability and merit."

vision-nz.evidence: "Completely remove all race-based targeted policies and spending within the healthcare sector"; "End all race-based politics."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Te Aka Motuhake" — an autonomous, state-funded, iwi-governed Māori health authority.

statements.text: A recent law that requires every new piece of legislation to be checked against a fixed list of "good regulation" principles, including protecting private property rights, should be scrapped.
statements.explainer: The law sets up a board to report on whether new laws meet principles such as the rule of law, protection of property and compensation when rules reduce property values. Supporters say it stops bad regulation; opponents say it privileges property owners over the environment and the Treaty and lets an unelected board second-guess Parliament.

national.evidence: Voted for the Bill at all three readings; did not answer Greenpeace's repeal question.

labour.evidence: Lodged a member's bill to repeal it (Nov 2025); "Yes" to repealing it in the Greenpeace survey.

green.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

act.evidence: Wrote and sponsored the Act (David Seymour, Minister for Regulation).

nz-first.evidence: Mixed: voted for it in 2025, Winston Peters then said NZ First would repeal it, but its 2026 Greenpeace survey answer did not commit to repeal.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "As a matter of priority, vote to repeal both the Regulatory Standards Act 2025 and the Treaty Clauses Review."

statements.text: Political donations should be capped, and only individual New Zealand voters should be allowed to donate.
statements.explainer: There is currently no limit on how much a person can give to a party, and companies, trusts and unions can donate. Caps and a voters-only rule reduce the influence of wealthy donors; opponents say they restrict free participation and favour parties with many small donors.

labour.evidence: No commitment: "Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations" (Greenpeace survey).

green.evidence: "Yes"; also "capping a donor's donations at a level that does not risk donor influence over policy."

nz-first.evidence: Supports "electoral integrity and transparency" but has no policy restricting donations to voters (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to limiting donations to registered voters (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Cap donations at $30,000 per donor per election and ban donations from companies and trusts.

animal-justice.evidence: Committed to "getting money out of politics" (no specific cap stated).

statements.text: Central government should cap how much councils can raise rates each year.
statements.explainer: Rates are the main income for local councils and have been rising well above inflation. A cap protects ratepayers but leaves councils with less money for water pipes, roads and other infrastructure unless they are given other funding tools.

national.evidence: Instruct councils to keep annual rate increases between 2 and 4 percent.

labour.evidence: Mixed: Barbara Edmonds said Labour supported the rates-cap bill to its first reading, while Tangi Utikere said in Dec 2025 "we don't support this rates cap" (both as quoted by National).

green.evidence: Reject the proposed rates cap and allow councils to use more funding tools.

opportunity.evidence: Give councils more tools to invest in infrastructure (rather than limiting revenue).

statements.text: Overall immigration to New Zealand should be reduced.
statements.explainer: Migration adds workers, students and skills but also pressure on housing and infrastructure. Lower immigration eases that pressure; employers say it worsens labour shortages and slows growth.

green.evidence: Increase the refugee quota and support migrant workers to residency.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled visa; remove automatic student-visa work rights; tie immigration to genuine labour shortages.

conservative.evidence: Cap net immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers (zero if social goods are not increasing), while welcoming skilled migrants.

vision-nz.evidence: "Pause mass immigration immediately to review visa policies and relieve pressure on local infrastructure."

statements.text: New residents should have to wait longer (five years or more) before they can get most benefits.
statements.explainer: Most benefits currently require two years' residence. A longer wait saves money and is argued to attract migrants who will not need support; critics say it leaves families with no safety net if they lose work.

national.evidence: Change entitlements for benefits for new NZ residents to five years.

act.evidence: "ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for residence class visa holders" (2026 Fiscal Plan).

nz-first.evidence: A benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants, and longer residency for citizenship.

statements.text: The age for receiving NZ Superannuation should stay at 65.
statements.explainer: Super is paid to everyone from 65 regardless of income or wealth. Keeping 65 is the status quo; raising it (for example gradually to 67) saves billions as the population ages but is hardest on people in physical jobs and those with shorter life expectancy.

national.evidence: Would "have liked to make change" and has long backed 67 from a future date, but its 2026 election policy is only to hold cross-party accord talks on the retirement system.

labour.evidence: "Labour has been clear that it will not means test New Zealand superannuation or increase the age of eligibility."

green.evidence: "Yes. We will retain NZ Superannuation as a universal entitlement from age 65."

act.evidence: Raise the retirement age to 67 by 2035 (three months a year).

nz-first.evidence: "New Zealand First will not support changes to the entitlement or eligibility of New Zealand Superannuation."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Says the age of eligibility "should not be raised at all" and should be lower for Māori because of lower life expectancy (May 2023 statement; no newer position found).

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to retaining the eligibility age at 65 (Grey Power survey).

alliance.evidence: "Keeps the age of entitlement for Super at 65."

statements.text: Main benefits (such as Jobseeker and Sole Parent Support) should be substantially increased.
statements.explainer: Benefit rates are adjusted each year and many recipients are below the poverty line. Larger increases reduce hardship directly but cost more and, some argue, reduce the incentive to work.

national.evidence: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than two years.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan has no benefit increases; it tightens eligibility (independent medical certification for health and disability benefits, a five-year stand-down for new residents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions and ensure everybody is paid enough to live with dignity, whether they are in employment or not" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: A universal Citizens' Income of up to $370 a week, replacing many main benefits.

alliance.evidence: Proposes a Universal Benefit, individual entitlements, universal child payments and an end to benefit sanctions.

womens-rights.evidence: "Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "complex, punitive benefit system" with a non-taxable Universal Whānau Allowance and wipe MSD/IRD debt for low-income whānau.

statements.text: People on benefits should face tougher obligations and sanctions, such as drug testing or payment cuts if they do not meet requirements.
statements.explainer: Sanctions reduce or suspend payments when obligations such as job-seeking are not met. Supporters say they move people into work; opponents say they punish children and people with health problems and do little to create jobs.

national.evidence: Introduce drug testing for people receiving benefits; reduce payments after two years on a benefit; longer stand-downs.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries; refuse to use AI for welfare decisions.

act.evidence: Restrict medical certification for health-related benefits and monitor spending of long-term jobseekers.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions"; called the traffic-light sanctions system "a tool designed to punish whānau" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: Citizen's Income replaces most main benefits: "no Work and Income appointments, no relationship status checks—just a guaranteed payment".

alliance.evidence: "An end to benefit sanctions."

conservative.evidence: "Welfare: Reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass."

vision-nz.evidence: "Dismantle state dependency"; "Slash state dependency by eliminating financial rules that disincentivise marriage."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "punitive benefit system" and end "relationship status" policing.

statements.text: Transport money should go mainly to public transport, cycling and rail rather than new highways.
statements.explainer: The national transport fund is limited, so spending on big new highways competes with buses, trains and cycleways. Roads suit freight and regions; public transport suits cities and reduces emissions and congestion.

national.evidence: Complete construction of the next set of Roads of National Significance; fund the $800m Christchurch Northern Motorway extension.

labour.evidence: Introduce a $20 weekly public-transport fare cap in the main cities ($10 elsewhere).

green.evidence: Build mass rapid transit in three major cities and invest in better rail and bus links; free or $2 fares.

act.evidence: Focus the National Land Transport Fund on road infrastructure only.

nz-first.evidence: Establish a 12-month trial of commuter rail in Canterbury and further south.

opportunity.evidence: Make public transport free.

alliance.evidence: Publicly owned rail and coastal shipping as "twin backbones" of freight, more public-transport funding.

statements.text: Rules limiting farm pollution of rivers (such as limits on nitrogen fertiliser and stock numbers) should be strengthened rather than loosened.
statements.explainer: Many rivers and lakes fail swimming or ecological standards, largely from farm run-off. Tighter rules improve water quality over time but raise costs for farmers; looser rules do the reverse.

national.evidence: Supported blocking regional freshwater plans and let restrictions on intensification lapse (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Says "freshwater limits should be national bottom lines" and wants councils able to implement the 2020 freshwater policy, but would not commit to lowering the nitrogen cap.

green.evidence: Impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices; phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser.

act.evidence: Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes.

nz-first.evidence: "No. Our approach is for practical, science-based freshwater management that balances environmental outcomes with productive land use."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to immediately lowering the synthetic nitrogen fertiliser cap and banning new dairy conversions (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Tighten rules on water quality and reinstate Te Mana o te Wai, but did not back a lower fertiliser cap.

animal-justice.evidence: Links intensive dairying to "degradation of waterways"; seeks to transition away from animal agriculture.

statements.text: Rules on gene technology (genetic modification) should be relaxed so modified crops and organisms can be used outside the laboratory.
statements.explainer: Gene editing is currently effectively confined to the lab. Relaxing the rules could bring faster-growing crops, pest control and medical uses; opponents worry about the environment and about the "GM-free" image of New Zealand exports.

national.evidence: The Gene Technology Bill is a National-led government bill; National remains in favour (it lacks NZ First's votes to pass).

labour.evidence: Withheld support at select committee citing limited consultation and lack of regulatory independence.

green.evidence: Called the Bill a "radical liberalisation and deregulation of GM technology" and withheld support.

act.evidence: Supports the Gene Technology Bill (with objections to its Māori advisory committee).

nz-first.evidence: Would not support the Bill into law without major changes, calling it "far too liberal" and lacking safeguards.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Told RNZ it "remained opposed to the bill".

opportunity.evidence: Rewrite gene technology regulations to enable modern gene technologies.

conservative.evidence: "We oppose the current government's move to end the long-standing restrictions placed on field trials and the release of genetically modified organisms."

statements.text: New Zealand should formally recognise the State of Palestine now.
statements.explainer: Recognition is a diplomatic step many countries, including Australia, Canada and the UK, have taken. Supporters see it as backing a two-state solution; opponents say it should wait for a negotiated settlement.

national.evidence: Government (PM Luxon, Foreign Minister Peters) decided in Sept 2025 not to recognise Palestine "yet", calling recognition inevitable but premature while Hamas remains.

labour.evidence: "Labour will recognise the State of Palestine" and place economic sanctions on Israel.

green.evidence: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel.

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters announced at the UN in Sept 2025: "we do not think that time is now."

alliance.evidence: "We must demand self-determination for Palestinians and the right to return to their homeland."

free-palestine.evidence: Party exists to press NZ to "uphold its obligations under international law with respect to Palestine"; seeks a single democratic state.

statements.text: Defence spending should rise substantially, towards 2% of GDP.
statements.explainer: Defence spending is currently about 1% of national income. Doubling it over a decade means billions more for ships, aircraft and personnel, and less for other priorities, in return for a stronger military and closer alignment with allies.

national.evidence: National-led government's Defence Capability Plan targets 2% of GDP by 2032/33; Defence Minister Chris Penk reaffirmed "a smooth and steady upward trajectory to 2 percent" in May 2026.

green.evidence: Security policy prioritises peacekeeping and "prevention over military force" and would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes network; no increase in military spending proposed.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan cuts non-frontline spending but protects "the spending growth since 2017 in core frontline services such as health, education, defence" (no specific 2% target found in its 2026 documents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Declare NZ a "military neutral" country and focus the Defence Force on protection, disaster response and the Pacific.

alliance.evidence: A "peace-focused defence force", non-alignment and an end to intelligence sharing with the US.

free-palestine.evidence: NZ should withdraw "from any formal security alliances with the U.S." and distance itself from "military interventionism".

statements.text: New Zealand should increase its overseas aid budget.
statements.explainer: Aid is about a quarter to a third of a percent of national income; the UN target is 0.7%. More aid supports Pacific neighbours and global standing; opponents say money should stay at home while there are needs here.

labour.evidence: Increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of GDP.

green.evidence: Increase climate aid funding to the Pacific.

act.evidence: Reduce NZ's foreign aid to 2017 levels.

alliance.evidence: Developed nations should cancel Global South debts "as a form of reparation".

statements.text: Cannabis should be legalised or decriminalised for personal use.
statements.explainer: Possession is currently a crime, though police mostly use discretion. Legalising or decriminalising would end convictions for personal use and could be taxed and regulated; opponents point to health harms and youth use. A 2020 referendum narrowly rejected legalisation.

green.evidence: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use; long-term policy is a legal, regulated cannabis market.

opportunity.evidence: Decriminalise drug possession (but not supply).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "We do not believe cultivation or possession of cannabis for personal use should be a criminal offense."

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "That the possession, cultivation and use of pure cannabis... be free from prosecution" and a regulated R18 cannabis market.

statements.text: Children under 16 should be banned from social media.
statements.explainer: A ban would require platforms to verify ages and remove young users. Supporters cite mental health and online harm; opponents cite privacy risks of age checks, the practicality of enforcing it and parents' right to decide.

national.evidence: Ban under-16 year olds from social media (Online Safety (Minimum Age...) Bill).

labour.evidence: Backed the bill to pass its first reading and go to select committee, wanting it "substantially improved".

act.evidence: Will vote against: "The ban they propose won't work, and the side effects will leave us worse off" (David Seymour).

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters said NZ First would "never support this", citing a slippery slope.

opportunity.evidence: Support the online safety bill on an under-16 ban going to select committee.

statements.text: Puberty blockers and other medical gender-transition treatments should not be available to people under 18.
statements.explainer: Puberty blockers delay physical changes for young people with gender dysphoria. Restricting them follows some other countries' caution over evidence; opponents say the decision should rest with young people, families and doctors.

national.evidence: Health Minister Simeon Brown halted new puberty-blocker prescriptions for gender dysphoria from 19 Dec 2025 as a "precautionary approach".

green.evidence: Free access to gender-affirming health care "including reversal of the ban on puberty blockers".

nz-first.evidence: Campaigned for the ban and announced it ahead of the Ministry; Peters: "we never stopped fighting to make this happen."

conservative.evidence: Restrict irreversible procedures to alter a child's sex characteristics "where there is no clear medical necessity" and require independent assessment.

womens-rights.evidence: Supports the puberty-blocker ban and would extend it to cross-sex hormones for under-18s and surgery for under-25s.

vision-nz.evidence: "Prohibit all medical interventions for gender transition in minors."

statements.text: Abortion law should be made more restrictive.
statements.explainer: Abortion was removed from the Crimes Act in 2020 and is available on request up to 20 weeks, with conditions after that. More restriction means tighter time limits or extra requirements; most parties treat this as a conscience issue rather than party policy.

conservative.evidence: Introduce an Unborn Child (Legal Personhood and Rights) Act recognising an unborn child as a legal person from the third trimester (28 weeks).

womens-rights.evidence: Lists "the right to have control of our own bodies, including reproductive autonomy" among the rights it exists to protect.

vision-nz.evidence: Healthcare policy commits to "protecting the sanctity of human life" (no specific abortion law change stated).
